Pattern 17 of 24

Stack

Last in, first out. When the most recent unfinished thing is always the next one to finish (an open bracket, a pending operand, a score you might cancel), keep those things on a stack and work on its top.

1. What is this pattern for?

A stack of plates. You can only put a plate on top and only take the top plate off. The plate you'll grab next is always the one you put down most recently, and the first plate you put down is the last one you'll ever reach.

A stack is a list where you only touch one end: append to push, pop() to remove, stack[-1] to peek. All three are O(1). It fits any problem with nesting or undo, where the most recent open item must be closed first:

  • Matching pairs: brackets, HTML tags, function calls (the call stack itself!).
  • Expression evaluation: postfix / RPN, calculators, decoding 3[a2[c]].
  • Undo / cancel: "remove the previous score", browser back button, simplifying paths with ...
  • Augmented stacks: carry extra information with each entry (the minimum so far, a count).

When the stack is kept sorted to find the next greater/smaller element, that's the specialised Monotonic Stack pattern.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Decide what waits. Things that can't be resolved yet: open brackets, numbers waiting for an operator, valid scores.
  2. Push when something opens. stack.append(item).
  3. Resolve against the top when something closes. Peek with stack[-1] to check it matches, then pop(). An empty stack at that moment usually means invalid input.
  4. Check what's left at the end. Leftovers mean unclosed items (invalid brackets), or they are the answer (the final value, the remaining scores).

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot a Stack

Trigger words

  • "valid parentheses", "balanced", "matching", "well-formed"
  • "evaluate", "reverse Polish / postfix", "calculator", "decode the string"
  • "undo", "cancel the previous", "backspace", "simplify path"
  • "design a stack that also supports getMin / getMax in O(1)"
  • "nested", "innermost first", "most recent"

Shape of the input

  • A sequence of tokens where an earlier token is "closed" or "consumed" by a later one.
  • Nesting depth that can be arbitrary: you can't solve it with a fixed number of variables.
  • Brute-force smell: repeatedly scanning backwards for "the last unmatched thing".
The one question to ask"Is the thing I need to deal with next always the most recent thing that is still open?" If yes, it belongs on a stack.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use a stack when…Prefer something else when…
The most recent open item must be resolved first (LIFO)The oldest item goes first (FIFO): use a queue (collections.deque), as in BFS
You match or evaluate nested structureOnly one kind of bracket and you just need validity: a single counter is enough
You must undo the last actionYou need the next greater/smaller element for every index: keep the stack sorted, that's Monotonic Stack
Simulating recursion without the call stack (iterative DFS / in-order traversal)Recursion depth is small and the recursive version is clearer: just recurse

Cost: every item is pushed and popped at most once, so O(n) time; up to O(n) space when everything stays open.

5. The templates, step by step (Python, TypeScript, Java)

A stack answers "what's the most recent unfinished thing?". Three templates: A matches brackets (the most recent opener must close first), B evaluates postfix expressions (the two most recent numbers meet each operator), C is a min-stack that remembers the minimum at every height, so get_min stays O(1) after pops.

Template A · Balanced brackets

The question it answersIs every bracket closed by the matching type, in the right order?
What it keepsA stack of openers still waiting to be closed.
When it checks for an answerEach closer must match the top opener; at the end the stack must be empty.
Use it whenValid parentheses (LC 20), remove invalid/minimum add to make valid, HTML/XML tag matching, decode string.
Not forA single bracket type where a counter is enough.
Memory hook: "The last door you opened is the first you must close"Walking into rooms inside rooms: you must leave through the doors in reverse order. A closer that doesn't match the most recent opened door, or doors still open at the end, means the building is broken.

The story, mapped to the code. Openers are doors you walk through; closers are doors you walk back out of.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Doors still openstackMost recent on top.
Walk through a doorstack.append(ch)An opener.
Walk out: must be the last doorstack[-1] == opener_of[ch]Matching type on top.
Nowhere to walk out tonot stackCloser with no opener.
Doors left openreturn not stackUnclosed openers.

The template. A dictionary from each closer to its opener keeps the checks short.

def is_balanced(s):
    opener_of = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in opener_of:
            if not stack or stack[-1] != opener_of[ch]:
                return False
            stack.pop()
        else:
            stack.append(ch)
    return not stack
function isBalanced(s: string): boolean {
  const openerOf: Record<string, string> = { ")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{" };
  const stack: string[] = [];
  for (const ch of s) {
    if (ch in openerOf) {
      if (stack.length === 0 || stack[stack.length - 1] !== openerOf[ch]) {
        return false;
      }
      stack.pop();
    } else {
      stack.push(ch);
    }
  }
  return stack.length === 0;
}
static boolean isBalanced(String s) {
    Map<Character, Character> openerOf = Map.of(')', '(', ']', '[', '}', '{');
    Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (openerOf.containsKey(ch)) {
            if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.peek() != openerOf.get(ch)) {
                return false;
            }
            stack.pop();
        } else {
            stack.push(ch);
        }
    }
    return stack.isEmpty();
}

Invariant. After each character, the stack holds the unmatched openers of the prefix, in order; the prefix is valid so far iff no mismatch has occurred.

Complexity. O(n) time, O(n) space.

Template B · Evaluate postfix (reverse Polish notation)

The question it answersCompute an expression written as operands then operator, e.g. 2 1 + 3 *.
What it keepsA stack of numbers waiting for an operator.
When it checks for an answerEach operator pops two numbers (right one first) and pushes the result.
Use it whenEvaluate RPN (LC 150); the inner loop of calculators (LC 224/227) after converting infix.
Not forInfix with precedence directly (needs two stacks or recursion).
Memory hook: "Numbers wait on a plate; an operator eats the top two"Numbers are stacked on a plate. When an operator arrives, it takes the top two (the top one is the right operand), combines them, and puts the result back.

The story, mapped to the code. The plate is the stack.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Put a number on the platestack.append(int(tok))Operand.
Take the right operandb = stack.pop()Popped first.
Take the left operanda = stack.pop()Popped second.
Put the result backstack.append(OPS[tok](a, b))Combined.
One number leftstack[0]The answer.

The template. A table of operations keeps the loop short. Division truncates toward zero (as LC 150 requires).

OPS = {"+": lambda a, b: a + b, "-": lambda a, b: a - b,
       "*": lambda a, b: a * b, "/": lambda a, b: int(a / b)}

def eval_postfix(tokens):
    stack = []
    for tok in tokens:
        if tok in OPS:
            b = stack.pop()
            a = stack.pop()
            stack.append(OPS[tok](a, b))
        else:
            stack.append(int(tok))
    return stack[0]
const OPS: Record<string, (a: number, b: number) => number> = {
  "+": (a, b) => a + b, "-": (a, b) => a - b,
  "*": (a, b) => a * b, "/": (a, b) => Math.trunc(a / b),
};

function evalPostfix(tokens: string[]): number {
  const stack: number[] = [];
  for (const tok of tokens) {
    if (tok in OPS) {
      const b = stack.pop()!;
      const a = stack.pop()!;
      stack.push(OPS[tok](a, b));
    } else {
      stack.push(Number(tok));
    }
  }
  return stack[0];
}
static int evalPostfix(String[] tokens) {
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (String tok : tokens) {
        if ("+-*/".contains(tok) && tok.length() == 1) {
            int b = stack.pop();
            int a = stack.pop();
            stack.push(switch (tok) {
                case "+" -> a + b;
                case "-" -> a - b;
                case "*" -> a * b;
                default -> a / b;
            });
        } else {
            stack.push(Integer.parseInt(tok));
        }
    }
    return stack.peek();
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
if tok in OPSOperator or number?Is it an eater?Checking tok[0] in '+-*/' treats "-3" as an operator.
b = stack.pop(); a = stack.pop()Right operand comes off first.Top of the plate is the right-hand number.Swapping them breaks − and ÷ (see the bug player).
OPS['/'] = int(a / b)Truncates toward zero.—a // b floors: −7 // 2 = −4, but the expected answer is −3.

Watch it run. Step through 5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 - (= 5 + (1 + 2) × 4 − 3). The second player pops the operands in the wrong order.

+ and × don't care about order, but at the final − the operands are reversed: 3 − 17 = −14 instead of 17 − 3 = 14.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. After each token, the stack holds the values of the complete sub-expressions read so far, left to right.

Complexity. O(n) time, O(n) space.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Operand order. Right operand pops first.
  • Floor division. Truncate toward zero.
  • Negative numbers mistaken for operators. Match the whole token.

Template C · Min stack (minimum at every height)

The question it answersA stack with push, pop, top and get_min, all O(1).
What it keepsEach entry stores its value and the minimum of everything at or below it.
When it checks for an answer—
Use it whenMin Stack (LC 155), max stack, stack-based undo with "best so far".
Not forMin over a sliding window (monotonic deque).
Memory hook: "Every plate remembers the smallest plate under it"When you add a plate, write on it the smallest number in the pile so far (its own or the one written on the plate below). Popping a plate reveals the plate below, which already knows the minimum for the smaller pile.

The story, mapped to the code. Each stack entry is a pair (value, minimum so far).

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
The plate(x, low)Value and the pile's minimum at this height.
Write the minimum on itlow = min(x, stack[-1][1])Its own or the one below.
Lift a platestack.pop()The plate below still knows its minimum.
Read the top plate's notestack[-1][1]get_min in O(1).

The template. Store pairs; nothing else changes.

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []

    def push(self, x):
        low = min(x, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else x
        self.stack.append((x, low))

    def pop(self):
        self.stack.pop()

    def top(self):
        return self.stack[-1][0]

    def get_min(self):
        return self.stack[-1][1]
class MinStack {
  stack: [number, number][] = [];

  push(x: number): void {
    const low = this.stack.length ? Math.min(x, this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][1]) : x;
    this.stack.push([x, low]);
  }

  pop(): void {
    this.stack.pop();
  }

  top(): number {
    return this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][0];
  }

  getMin(): number {
    return this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][1];
  }
}
static class MinStack {
    private final Deque<int[]> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void push(int x) {
        int low = stack.isEmpty() ? x : Math.min(x, stack.peek()[1]);
        stack.push(new int[]{x, low});
    }

    void pop() {
        stack.pop();
    }

    int top() {
        return stack.peek()[0];
    }

    int getMin() {
        return stack.peek()[1];
    }
}

All three use the stack for "the most recent unfinished thing": the last opened door, the last two values, the minimum of the current pile. For "next greater/smaller" questions, see the monotonic stack (page 6).

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Plates in the cafeteria"The last plate put down is the first one picked up. Whatever opened most recently closes first.
How this hook works: what “Plates in the cafeteria” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Plates in the cafeteria”
A stack: you add to and take from the top only.
“The last plate put down is the first one picked up”
Last in, first out (LIFO): append and pop both work at the end of the list.
“Whatever opened most recently closes first”
Why it fits brackets, nested calls and undo: the innermost open thing must be finished before anything outside it.

Why this picture fits the pattern: Stack problems all have nesting: brackets inside brackets, expressions inside expressions, decode-string layers. The plate stack always keeps the most recent unfinished thing on top.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
Put a plate downstack.append(ch) for an opener
Look at the top platestack[-1]
Pick up the top platestack.pop() when the closer matches
Empty tray at the endreturn not stack

Watch it on numbers

Is "([]{})" balanced? And "([)]"?

  1. ( and [ go down. Then ] arrives and the top is [, a match, so pick it up.
  2. { goes down, } matches it. Then ) matches the (. The tray is empty: balanced.
  3. "([)]": ( and [ go down, then ) arrives but the top plate is [. Mismatch: not balanced. Merely counting brackets would have said yes.

The trap it saves you from

Peeking at an empty stack ("]" alone → IndexError), and forgetting the final "is it empty?" check ("((" would pass). In postfix evaluation, the top plate is the right operand: pop b, then a, then compute a / b.

It still works when…

Min Stack: each plate carries the minimum so far. Decode String: on [, put the current string and count on the stack; on ], pick them up and combine.

Picture

Russian dolls: you can't close the outer doll until every doll inside it is closed.

Chant

"Open: push. Close: peek, match, pop. End: empty?"

Order rule

"Pop b, then a." The top of the stack is the right operand.

Easy 20. Valid Parentheses Start here Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft StringStack

Problem: s contains only ()[]{}. It is valid if every bracket is closed by the same type, in the correct order. Check it.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "()"
Output: true
Example 2
Input: s = "()[]{}"
Output: true

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁴ · s consists of parentheses only '()[]{}'.

Hint 1

The most recently opened bracket must close first.

Hint 2

Push openers; for a closer, the top of the stack must be the matching opener. At the end, the stack must be empty.

From brute force to the pattern: Repeatedly deleting (), [] and {} pairs from the string until nothing changes is O(n²). A stack matches each bracket once: O(n).

Spot it: "Most recent unmatched opener must close first" is last-in, first-out → a stack.

Approach:

  1. Map each closer to its opener: ) → (, ] → [, } → {.
  2. Push every opener.
  3. For a closer: the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener; pop it. Otherwise invalid.
  4. At the end, every opener must have been matched: the stack must be empty.
class Solution:
    def isValid(self, s: str) -> bool:
        opener_of = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
        stack = []
        for ch in s:
            if ch in opener_of:
                # a closer: it must close the most recent unmatched opener
                if not stack or stack[-1] != opener_of[ch]:
                    return False
                stack.pop()
            else:
                stack.append(ch)          # an opener waits for its closer
        # leftover openers were never closed
        return len(stack) == 0
function isValid(s: string): boolean {
    const openerOf: Record<string, string> = { ")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{" };
    const stack: string[] = [];
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch in openerOf) {
            // a closer: it must close the most recent unmatched opener
            if (stack.length === 0 || stack[stack.length - 1] !== openerOf[ch]) {
                return false;
            }
            stack.pop();
        } else {
            stack.push(ch);  // an opener waits for its closer
        }
    }
    // leftover openers were never closed
    return stack.length === 0;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean isValid(String s) {
        Map<Character, Character> openerOf = Map.of(')', '(', ']', '[', '}', '{');
        Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (openerOf.containsKey(ch)) {
                // a closer: it must close the most recent unmatched opener
                if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.peek() != openerOf.get(ch)) {
                    return false;
                }
                stack.pop();
            } else {
                stack.push(ch);  // an opener waits for its closer
            }
        }
        // leftover openers were never closed
        return stack.isEmpty();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. opener_of: for each closing bracket, the opening bracket it needs.
  2. if ch in opener_of: the character is a closer.
  3. if not stack or stack[-1] != opener_of[ch]: return False: nothing to close, or the wrong type on top, e.g. "(]".
  4. stack.pop(): the pair is matched and removed.
  5. stack.append(ch): openers wait on the stack.
  6. return len(stack) == 0: "((" has no bad closer but is still invalid.

Edge cases to test:

  • Only openers, e.g. "((" → False.
  • A closer first, e.g. ")(" → False.
  • Interleaved types, e.g. "([)]" → False.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 150. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation Google Meta Amazon ArrayStack

Problem: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation, where operators come after their two operands (["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"] means (2 + 1) * 3). Division truncates toward zero.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: tokens = ["2","1","+","3","*"]
Output: 9
Explanation: ((2 + 1) * 3) = 9
Example 2
Input: tokens = ["4","13","5","/","+"]
Output: 6
Explanation: (4 + (13 / 5)) = 6

Constraints: 1 ≤ tokens.length ≤ 10⁴ · tokens[i] is either an operator: "+", "-", "*", or "/", or an integer in the range [-200, 200].

Hint 1

Numbers wait until an operator arrives.

Hint 2

Push numbers; for an operator, pop b then a, push a op b. Truncate division toward zero.

From brute force to the pattern: Converting back to infix and evaluating is roundabout. A stack evaluates postfix in one pass: O(n).

Spot it: In postfix, an operator always applies to the two most recent results → stack evaluation.

Approach:

  1. Push numbers.
  2. For an operator: pop b (the top), then a. Compute a op b (order matters for - and /) and push the result.
  3. The single value left is the answer.
class Solution:
    def evalRPN(self, tokens: List[str]) -> int:
        stack = []
        for token in tokens:
            if token in ("+", "-", "*", "/"):
                b = stack.pop()       # the RIGHT operand is on top
                a = stack.pop()
                if token == "+":
                    stack.append(a + b)
                elif token == "-":
                    stack.append(a - b)
                elif token == "*":
                    stack.append(a * b)
                else:
                    # int(a / b) truncates toward zero; a // b would round down
                    stack.append(int(a / b))
            else:
                stack.append(int(token))
        return stack[0]
function evalRPN(tokens: string[]): number {
    const stack: number[] = [];
    for (const token of tokens) {
        if (token === "+" || token === "-" || token === "*" || token === "/") {
            const b = stack.pop()!;  // the RIGHT operand is on top
            const a = stack.pop()!;
            if (token === "+") {
                stack.push(a + b);
            } else if (token === "-") {
                stack.push(a - b);
            } else if (token === "*") {
                stack.push(a * b);
            } else {
                // Math.trunc truncates toward zero; Math.floor would round down
                stack.push(Math.trunc(a / b));
            }
        } else {
            stack.push(Number(token));
        }
    }
    return stack[0];
}
class Solution {
    public int evalRPN(String[] tokens) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (String token : tokens) {
            if (token.equals("+") || token.equals("-") || token.equals("*") || token.equals("/")) {
                int b = stack.pop();  // the RIGHT operand is on top
                int a = stack.pop();
                if (token.equals("+")) {
                    stack.push(a + b);
                } else if (token.equals("-")) {
                    stack.push(a - b);
                } else if (token.equals("*")) {
                    stack.push(a * b);
                } else {
                    // Java's / already truncates toward zero
                    stack.push(a / b);
                }
            } else {
                stack.push(Integer.parseInt(token));
            }
        }
        return stack.peek();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if token in ("+", "-", "*", "/"): an operator; anything else is a number (possibly negative, like "-11").
  2. b = stack.pop() then a = stack.pop(): the top is the second operand. ["4", "2", "-"] means 4 − 2, not 2 − 4.
  3. int(a / b): LeetCode wants truncation toward zero. Python's // floors, so -7 // 2 is -4, while int(-7 / 2) is -3.
  4. return stack[0]: a valid expression leaves exactly one value.

Dry run on the example:

tokens = ["4", "13", "5", "/", "+"] (LeetCode Example 2). Returns 6 (4 + 13 / 5).

tokenactionstack after
"4"push[4]
"13"push[4, 13]
"5"push[4, 13, 5]
"/"int(13 / 5) = 2[4, 2]
"+"4 + 2 = 6[6]

Edge cases to test:

  • Negative numbers like "-11" (not an operator!).
  • Division truncating toward zero, e.g. -7 / 2 → -3.
  • A single number.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Medium 155. Min Stack Start here Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Stack

Problem: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and getMin (the smallest element currently in the stack), all in O(1) time.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: ["MinStack","push","push","push","getMin","pop","top","getMin"] [[],[-2],[0],[-3],[],[],[],[]]
Output: [null,null,null,null,-3,null,0,-2]
Explanation: MinStack minStack = new MinStack(); minStack.push(-2); minStack.push(0); minStack.push(-3); minStack.getMin(); // return -3 minStack.pop(); minStack.top(); // return 0 minStack.getMin(); // return -2

Constraints: -2³¹ ≤ val ≤ 2³¹ - 1 · Methods pop, top and getMin operations will always be called on non-empty stacks. · At most 3 * 10⁴ calls will be made to push, pop, top, and getMin.

Hint 1

After popping the minimum, you need the previous minimum immediately.

Hint 2

Store, with each entry, the minimum of everything at or below it.

From brute force to the pattern: Scanning the stack for the minimum is O(n) per getMin. Keeping the running minimum with every entry makes all four operations O(1).

Spot it: Popping can remove the current minimum, and then you need the previous one immediately. So remember, for every position, what the minimum was at that height: push pairs (value, min so far).

Approach:

  1. Each stack entry is a pair (val, current_min).
  2. push(val): the new minimum is min(val, previous min) (or val if the stack is empty).
  3. pop() removes the top pair; the pair below still holds the correct minimum for the smaller stack.
  4. top() and getMin() read the two halves of the top pair.
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        # each entry is (value, smallest value at or below this entry)
        self.stack = []

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        if self.stack:
            current_min = min(val, self.stack[-1][1])
        else:
            current_min = val
        self.stack.append((val, current_min))

    def pop(self) -> None:
        self.stack.pop()

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][0]

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][1]
class MinStack {
    // each entry is [value, smallest value at or below this entry]
    private stack: [number, number][] = [];

    push(val: number): void {
        let currentMin: number;
        if (this.stack.length > 0) {
            currentMin = Math.min(val, this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][1]);
        } else {
            currentMin = val;
        }
        this.stack.push([val, currentMin]);
    }

    pop(): void {
        this.stack.pop();
    }

    top(): number {
        return this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][0];
    }

    getMin(): number {
        return this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][1];
    }
}
class MinStack {
    // each entry is (value, smallest value at or below this entry)
    private final Deque<int[]> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public MinStack() {
    }

    public void push(int val) {
        int currentMin;
        if (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            currentMin = Math.min(val, stack.peek()[1]);
        } else {
            currentMin = val;
        }
        stack.push(new int[] {val, currentMin});
    }

    public void pop() {
        stack.pop();
    }

    public int top() {
        return stack.peek()[0];
    }

    public int getMin() {
        return stack.peek()[1];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. self.stack: a list of tuples. self.stack[-1][0] is the top value, self.stack[-1][1] the minimum of the whole stack.
  2. push: the minimum for the new height is the smaller of val and the minimum just below.
  3. pop: no recomputation. The entry below already knows its own minimum.
  4. top, getMin: one index each, so O(1).

Edge cases to test:

  • Pushing duplicates of the minimum.
  • Popping the minimum.
  • Negative values.

Complexity: O(1) time for every operation, O(n) space.

8. Common mistakes

Popping an empty stackstack.pop() or stack[-1] on an empty list raises IndexError. Check if not stack first; for brackets, an empty stack at a closer means "invalid".
Forgetting the final check"((" never hits a bad closer, but it isn't valid. Return not stack, not just True.
Operand orderFor - and /, the first value popped is the right operand: ["4", "2", "-"] is 4 − 2.
Python division// floors toward −∞ (-7 // 2 == -4). Problems that say "truncate toward zero" need int(a / b).
Recomputing the minimum on popScanning the stack for the new minimum makes pop O(n). Store the running minimum with each entry instead.

9. Self-check quiz

All characters of "(()" are processed without a mismatch. What should the function return?

One ( is never closed, so the stack isn't empty at the end.

Evaluate the RPN tokens ["5", "3", "-", "2", "/"] (truncating division).

5 − 3 = 2, then 2 / 2 = 1. The first popped value is always the right operand.

How does Min Stack keep getMin() at O(1) even after popping the current minimum?

The entry below the popped one already recorded the minimum of the smaller stack.

Tasks must be processed in the order they arrived. Which structure?

Arrival order is first in, first out: a queue. A stack would always serve the newest task first.

Easy 682. Baseball Game Start here Meta ArrayStack

Problem: Process the operations: an integer records that score; "+" records the sum of the previous two scores; "D" records double the previous score; "C" removes the previous score. Return the total.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: ops = ["5","2","C","D","+"]
Output: 30
Explanation: "5" - Add 5 to the record, record is now [5]. "2" - Add 2 to the record, record is now [5, 2]. "C" - Invalidate and remove the previous score, record is now [5]. "D" - Add 2 * 5 = 10 to the record, record is now [5, 10]. "+" - Add 5 + 10 = 15 to the record, record is now [5, 10, 15]. The total sum is 5 + 10 + 15 = 30.
Example 2
Input: ops = ["5","-2","4","C","D","9","+","+"]
Output: 27
Explanation: "5" - Add 5 to the record, record is now [5]. "-2" - Add -2 to the record, record is now [5, -2]. "4" - Add 4 to the record, record is now [5, -2, 4]. "C" - Invalidate and remove the previous score, record is now [5, -2]. "D" - Add 2 * -2 = -4 to the record, record is now [5, -2, -4]. "9" - Add 9 to the record, record is now [5, -2, -4, 9]. "+" - Add -4 + 9 = 5 to the record, record is now [5, -2, -4, 9, 5]. "+" - Add 9 + 5 = 14 to the record, record is now [5, -2, -4, 9, 5, 14]. The total sum is 5 + -2 + -4 + 9 + 5 + 14 = 27.

Constraints: 1 ≤ operations.length ≤ 1000 · operations[i] is "C", "D", "+", or a string representing an integer in the range [-3 * 10⁴, 3 * 10⁴]. · For operation "+", there will always be at least two previous scores on the record. · For operations "C" and "D", there will always be at least one previous score on the record.

Hint 1

Every operation looks at the most recent valid scores.

Hint 2

Use a stack: C pops, D pushes double the top, + pushes the sum of the top two.

From brute force to the pattern: Keeping a plain list and re-reading it works the same way. The stack view makes it clear that only the top entries ever matter: O(n).

Spot it: Every operation refers to the most recent scores, and C undoes the last one. Recent-first access + undo = a stack.

Approach:

  1. C → pop. D → push 2 × top. + → push the sum of the top two.
  2. Otherwise push int(op).
  3. Return the sum of the stack.
class Solution:
    def calPoints(self, operations: List[str]) -> int:
        scores = []
        for op in operations:
            if op == "C":
                scores.pop()                         # cancel the last score
            elif op == "D":
                scores.append(2 * scores[-1])        # double the last score
            elif op == "+":
                scores.append(scores[-1] + scores[-2])
            else:
                scores.append(int(op))               # a plain number, maybe negative
        return sum(scores)
function calPoints(operations: string[]): number {
    const scores: number[] = [];
    for (const op of operations) {
        if (op === "C") {
            scores.pop();  // cancel the last score
        } else if (op === "D") {
            scores.push(2 * scores[scores.length - 1]);  // double the last score
        } else if (op === "+") {
            scores.push(scores[scores.length - 1] + scores[scores.length - 2]);
        } else {
            scores.push(Number(op));  // a plain number, maybe negative
        }
    }
    return scores.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
class Solution {
    public int calPoints(String[] operations) {
        List<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String op : operations) {
            int n = scores.size();
            if (op.equals("C")) {
                scores.remove(n - 1);  // cancel the last score
            } else if (op.equals("D")) {
                scores.add(2 * scores.get(n - 1));  // double the last score
            } else if (op.equals("+")) {
                scores.add(scores.get(n - 1) + scores.get(n - 2));
            } else {
                scores.add(Integer.parseInt(op));  // a plain number, maybe negative
            }
        }
        int total = 0;
        for (int x : scores) {
            total += x;
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. scores: valid scores so far; scores[-1] is the most recent and scores[-2] the one before it.
  2. scores.pop(): C removes the last score as if it never happened.
  3. 2 * scores[-1] and scores[-1] + scores[-2]: read the top without removing anything.
  4. int(op): converts strings such as "-2" to integers.
  5. sum(scores): the total of what remains.

"2"push 2[5, 2]
"C"pop 2[5]
"D"push 2 × 5[5, 10]
"+"push 10 + 5[5, 10, 15] → sum 30

Edge cases to test:

  • C removing the only score.
  • Negative scores.
  • + right after a C.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Medium 394. Decode String Google Meta Amazon Cisco StringStack

Problem: Decode a string encoded as k[encoded_string], where the part inside the brackets is repeated k times. Brackets can be nested, e.g. "3[a2[c]]" → "accaccacc".

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "3[a]2[bc]"
Output: "aaabcbc"
Example 2
Input: s = "3[a2[c]]"
Output: "accaccacc"

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 30 · s consists of lowercase English letters, digits, and square brackets '[]'. · s is guaranteed to be a valid input. · All the integers in s are in the range [1, 300].

Hint 1

When you meet ], which [ does it close, and which text was being built before that [?

Hint 2

Push the outer text and the repeat count when you see [; pop them when you see ].

From brute force to the pattern: Repeatedly finding the innermost k[...] with a search and replacing it rescans the string many times: O(n²) or worse. A stack processes each character once and expands each bracket exactly when it closes.

Spot it: Nested brackets where the innermost part must be finished first, then plugged into the level around it: last opened, first closed. That's a stack, just like matching parentheses, but each level also remembers its text and its repeat count.

Why not another pattern? A single left-to-right pass with string concatenation can't handle nesting, because when an inner ] closes you need the text that was being built outside it. Recursion works too (it uses the call stack); the explicit stack shows the same idea step by step.

Key insight: Keep two things while scanning: current (the string being built at this nesting level) and number (a repeat count being read). On [ push (current, number) and start a fresh level. On ] pop (previous, k) and set current = previous + current * k.

Approach:

  1. Scan characters. Digits build number (it can have several digits, e.g. 12[).
  2. On [: push (current, number), then reset current = "" and number = 0 for the inner level.
  3. On ]: pop (previous, k) and combine: current = previous + current * k.
  4. Any other character is a letter: append it to current.
  5. At the end, current is the decoded string.
class Solution:
    def decodeString(self, s: str) -> str:
        stack = []      # (text before this bracket, how many times to repeat it)
        current = ""    # text being built at the current nesting level
        number = 0      # repeat count being read digit by digit
        for ch in s:
            if ch.isdigit():
                number = number * 10 + int(ch)  # counts can have several digits
            elif ch == "[":
                stack.append((current, number))  # save the outer level
                current = ""  # start a fresh inner level
                number = 0
            elif ch == "]":
                previous, k = stack.pop()  # back to the outer level
                current = previous + current * k  # plug in the repeated inner text
            else:
                current = current + ch  # a plain letter
        return current
function decodeString(s: string): string {
    const stack: [string, number][] = [];  // [text before this bracket, how many times to repeat it]
    let current = "";  // text being built at the current nesting level
    let number = 0;    // repeat count being read digit by digit
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch >= "0" && ch <= "9") {
            number = number * 10 + Number(ch);  // counts can have several digits
        } else if (ch === "[") {
            stack.push([current, number]);  // save the outer level
            current = "";  // start a fresh inner level
            number = 0;
        } else if (ch === "]") {
            const [previous, k] = stack.pop()!;  // back to the outer level
            current = previous + current.repeat(k);  // plug in the repeated inner text
        } else {
            current = current + ch;  // a plain letter
        }
    }
    return current;
}
class Solution {
    public String decodeString(String s) {
        Deque<String> textStack = new ArrayDeque<>();   // text before this bracket
        Deque<Integer> countStack = new ArrayDeque<>(); // how many times to repeat it
        String current = "";  // text being built at the current nesting level
        int number = 0;       // repeat count being read digit by digit
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isDigit(ch)) {
                number = number * 10 + (ch - '0');  // counts can have several digits
            } else if (ch == '[') {
                textStack.push(current);  // save the outer level
                countStack.push(number);
                current = "";  // start a fresh inner level
                number = 0;
            } else if (ch == ']') {
                String previous = textStack.pop();  // back to the outer level
                int k = countStack.pop();
                current = previous + current.repeat(k);  // plug in the repeated inner text
            } else {
                current = current + ch;  // a plain letter
            }
        }
        return current;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. stack: each entry remembers the outer level's text and the count for the bracket we just entered.
  2. number = number * 10 + int(ch): builds multi-digit counts like 12 from '1' then '2'.
  3. [: push (current, number), then clear both. The inner level starts with empty text.
  4. ]: previous, k = stack.pop() restores the outer text; current * k repeats the inner text k times; previous + ... attaches it.
  5. else: a letter is appended to the current level.
  6. return current: after the last character we are back at the outermost level.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Multi-digit counts, e.g. "10[a]".
  • Letters after a bracket, e.g. "2[abc]3[cd]ef".
  • Deep nesting, e.g. "3[a2[c]]" → "accaccacc".

Complexity: O(output length) time and space: each character of the result is created once per nesting level that repeats it.

Medium 71. Simplify Path Google Meta Amazon Microsoft StringStack

Problem: Convert an absolute Unix path into its canonical form.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: path = "/home/"
Output: "/home"
Explanation: The trailing slash should be removed.
Example 2
Input: path = "/home//foo/"
Output: "/home/foo"
Explanation: Multiple consecutive slashes are replaced by a single one.

Constraints: 1 ≤ path.length ≤ 3000 · path consists of English letters, digits, period '.', slash '/' or '_'. · path is a valid absolute Unix path.

Hint 1

Split the path into parts.

Hint 2

Which parts add a directory, which remove one, which do nothing?

From brute force to the pattern: Repeated string replacement is fragile; a stack of parts is one clean pass.

Spot it: Directories nest: .. undoes the most recent directory → a stack of path parts.

Why not another pattern? String replacement tricks (/./, /../) get edge cases wrong (e.g. ... is a valid name).

Approach:

  1. Split by /.
  2. Skip empty parts and .; .. pops if possible; anything else is pushed.
  3. Join as / + /.join(stack).
class Solution:
    def simplifyPath(self, path: str) -> str:
        stack = []
        for part in path.split("/"):
            if part == "" or part == ".":
                continue  # extra slashes or "current directory"
            if part == "..":
                if stack:
                    stack.pop()  # go up one level
            else:
                stack.append(part)  # a directory name (even "...")
        return "/" + "/".join(stack)
function simplifyPath(path: string): string {
    const stack: string[] = [];
    for (const part of path.split("/")) {
        if (part === "" || part === ".") {
            continue;  // extra slashes or "current directory"
        }
        if (part === "..") {
            if (stack.length > 0) {
                stack.pop();  // go up one level
            }
        } else {
            stack.push(part);  // a directory name (even "...")
        }
    }
    return "/" + stack.join("/");
}
class Solution {
    public String simplifyPath(String path) {
        List<String> stack = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String part : path.split("/")) {
            if (part.isEmpty() || part.equals(".")) {
                continue;  // extra slashes or "current directory"
            }
            if (part.equals("..")) {
                if (!stack.isEmpty()) {
                    stack.remove(stack.size() - 1);  // go up one level
                }
            } else {
                stack.add(part);  // a directory name (even "...")
            }
        }
        return "/" + String.join("/", stack);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Multiple slashes produce empty parts, which are ignored.
  2. .. at the root stays at the root.
  3. Any other string, including ..., is a name.

Edge cases to test:

  • /../ → /.
  • Trailing slash.
  • Names like ....

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Medium 227. Basic Calculator II Google Meta Amazon Apple StringStack

Problem: Evaluate an expression with + − × / (integer division truncating toward zero) and spaces.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "3+2*2"
Output: 7
Example 2
Input: s = " 3/2 "
Output: 1

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 3 * 10⁵ · s consists of integers and operators ('+', '-', '*', '/') separated by some number of spaces. · s represents a valid expression. · All the integers in the expression are non-negative integers in the range [0, 2³¹ - 1]. · The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

Hint 1

Multiplication and division happen before addition.

Hint 2

Keep a stack of terms to add; × and ÷ change the last term.

From brute force to the pattern: Multiple passes (first × ÷, then + −) with list rewriting work but are clumsier; the stack is one pass.

Spot it: Precedence: ×/÷ must happen before +/−. Keep a stack of terms: +/− push a new term; ×/÷ modify the last term. The answer is the sum.

Why not another pattern? Evaluating left to right ignores precedence.

Approach:

  1. Read numbers; when an operator (or the end) arrives, apply the previous operator to num.
  2. + push num, − push −num, × multiply top, / divide top (truncate).
  3. Return sum(stack).
class Solution:
    def calculate(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = []
        num = 0
        op = "+"  # operator before the current number
        for i, ch in enumerate(s):
            if ch.isdigit():
                num = num * 10 + int(ch)
            if (ch in "+-*/") or i == len(s) - 1:
                if op == "+":
                    stack.append(num)
                elif op == "-":
                    stack.append(-num)
                elif op == "*":
                    stack.append(stack.pop() * num)  # binds tighter: apply now
                else:
                    stack.append(int(stack.pop() / num))  # truncate toward zero
                op = ch
                num = 0
        return sum(stack)
function calculate(s: string): number {
    const stack: number[] = [];
    let num = 0;
    let op = "+";  // operator before the current number
    for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
        const ch = s[i];
        if (ch >= "0" && ch <= "9") {
            num = num * 10 + Number(ch);
        }
        if ("+-*/".includes(ch) || i === s.length - 1) {
            if (op === "+") {
                stack.push(num);
            } else if (op === "-") {
                stack.push(-num);
            } else if (op === "*") {
                stack.push(stack.pop()! * num);  // binds tighter: apply now
            } else {
                stack.push(Math.trunc(stack.pop()! / num));  // truncate toward zero
            }
            op = ch;
            num = 0;
        }
    }
    return stack.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
class Solution {
    public int calculate(String s) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int num = 0;
        char op = '+';  // operator before the current number
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char ch = s.charAt(i);
            if (Character.isDigit(ch)) {
                num = num * 10 + (ch - '0');
            }
            if ("+-*/".indexOf(ch) >= 0 || i == s.length() - 1) {
                if (op == '+') {
                    stack.push(num);
                } else if (op == '-') {
                    stack.push(-num);
                } else if (op == '*') {
                    stack.push(stack.pop() * num);  // binds tighter: apply now
                } else {
                    stack.push(stack.pop() / num);  // Java's / truncates toward zero
                }
                op = ch;
                num = 0;
            }
        }
        int total = 0;
        for (int x : stack) {
            total += x;
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

Medium 362. Design Hit Counter Google Apple QueueDeque

Problem: Record hits at timestamps (non-decreasing) and return the number of hits in the past 300 seconds.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: ["HitCounter","hit","hit","hit","getHits","hit","getHits","getHits"] [[],[1],[2],[3],[4],[300],[300],[301]]
Output: [null,null,null,null,3,null,4,3]
Explanation: At time 301 the hit at time 1 is more than 300 seconds old, so only 3 remain.

Constraints: 1 ≤ timestamp ≤ 2 * 10⁹ · All the calls are made in chronological order (timestamp is monotonically increasing) · At most 300 calls will be made to hit and getHits

Hint 1

Timestamps come in order. Where are the expired hits?

Hint 2

Use a queue and drop from the front.

From brute force to the pattern: Scanning every stored hit per query is linear; dropping expired hits from a queue is amortised constant. (Follow-up: two arrays of 300 buckets give O(1) memory per second.)

Spot it: Timestamps arrive in order, so old hits are always at the front: a queue (deque). Remove expired hits from the front, the rest is the answer. (Like a monotonic stack, the order of insertion does the work.)

Why not another pattern? Storing all hits and scanning them per query is O(total hits) each time.

Approach:

  1. hit(t): append t.
  2. getHits(t): pop from the front while front ≤ t − 300; return the length.
from collections import deque

class HitCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.hits = deque()  # timestamps in arrival order

    def hit(self, timestamp: int) -> None:
        self.hits.append(timestamp)

    def getHits(self, timestamp: int) -> int:
        while self.hits and self.hits[0] <= timestamp - 300:
            self.hits.popleft()  # older than 5 minutes
        return len(self.hits)
class HitCounter {
    private hits: number[] = [];  // timestamps in arrival order
    private head = 0;  // hits[head] is the oldest one kept (shift() would be O(n))

    hit(timestamp: number): void {
        this.hits.push(timestamp);
    }

    getHits(timestamp: number): number {
        while (this.head < this.hits.length && this.hits[this.head] <= timestamp - 300) {
            this.head += 1;  // older than 5 minutes
        }
        return this.hits.length - this.head;
    }
}
class HitCounter {
    private final Deque<Integer> hits = new ArrayDeque<>();  // timestamps in arrival order

    public HitCounter() {
    }

    public void hit(int timestamp) {
        hits.offer(timestamp);
    }

    public int getHits(int timestamp) {
        while (!hits.isEmpty() && hits.peek() <= timestamp - 300) {
            hits.poll();  // older than 5 minutes
        }
        return hits.size();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Expired hits are at the front because timestamps never decrease.
  2. Each hit is removed at most once, so the work is amortised O(1).

  • A query exactly 300 s later (excluded).
  • No hits yet → 0.

Complexity: Amortised O(1) per call, O(hits in window) space.

Medium 622. Design Circular Queue Google Nvidia Amazon Microsoft ArrayQueue

Problem: Implement a fixed-capacity FIFO ring buffer with enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, isFull.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: ["MyCircularQueue", "enQueue", "enQueue", "enQueue", "enQueue", "Rear", "isFull", "deQueue", "enQueue", "Rear"] [[3], [1], [2], [3], [4], [], [], [], [4], []]
Output: [null, true, true, true, false, 3, true, true, true, 4]
Explanation: MyCircularQueue myCircularQueue = new MyCircularQueue(3); myCircularQueue.enQueue(1); // return True myCircularQueue.enQueue(2); // return True myCircularQueue.enQueue(3); // return True myCircularQueue.enQueue(4); // return False myCircularQueue.Rear(); // return 3 myCircularQueue.isFull(); // return True myCircularQueue.deQueue(); // return True myCircularQueue.enQueue(4); // return True myCircularQueue.Rear(); // return 4

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ value ≤ 1000 · At most 3000 calls will be made to enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, and isFull.

Hint 1

Use a fixed-size array and wrap indices with modulo.

Hint 2

Track the head and the number of elements.

From brute force to the pattern: A list with pop(0) shifts every element; the ring buffer never moves data.

Spot it: A ring buffer is an array where indices wrap around. Store the head index and the count; the tail is (head + count − 1) % k.

Why not another pattern? A Python list with pop(0) is O(n) per dequeue and doesn't have a fixed capacity.

Approach:

  1. enQueue: if full, false; write at (head + size) % k, size += 1.
  2. deQueue: if empty, false; head = (head + 1) % k, size −= 1.
  3. Front = data[head], Rear = data[(head + size − 1) % k].
class MyCircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, k: int):
        self.data = [0] * k
        self.head = 0  # index of the front element
        self.size = 0

    def enQueue(self, value: int) -> bool:
        if self.size == len(self.data):
            return False
        self.data[(self.head + self.size) % len(self.data)] = value  # next free slot, wrapping
        self.size += 1
        return True

    def deQueue(self) -> bool:
        if self.size == 0:
            return False
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % len(self.data)  # the front moves forward
        self.size -= 1
        return True

    def Front(self) -> int:
        return self.data[self.head] if self.size else -1

    def Rear(self) -> int:
        return self.data[(self.head + self.size - 1) % len(self.data)] if self.size else -1

    def isEmpty(self) -> bool:
        return self.size == 0

    def isFull(self) -> bool:
        return self.size == len(self.data)
class MyCircularQueue {
    private data: number[];
    private head = 0;  // index of the front element
    private size = 0;

    constructor(k: number) {
        this.data = new Array(k).fill(0);
    }

    enQueue(value: number): boolean {
        if (this.size === this.data.length) {
            return false;
        }
        this.data[(this.head + this.size) % this.data.length] = value;  // next free slot, wrapping
        this.size += 1;
        return true;
    }

    deQueue(): boolean {
        if (this.size === 0) {
            return false;
        }
        this.head = (this.head + 1) % this.data.length;  // the front moves forward
        this.size -= 1;
        return true;
    }

    Front(): number {
        return this.size ? this.data[this.head] : -1;
    }

    Rear(): number {
        return this.size ? this.data[(this.head + this.size - 1) % this.data.length] : -1;
    }

    isEmpty(): boolean {
        return this.size === 0;
    }

    isFull(): boolean {
        return this.size === this.data.length;
    }
}
class MyCircularQueue {
    private final int[] data;
    private int head = 0;  // index of the front element
    private int size = 0;

    public MyCircularQueue(int k) {
        data = new int[k];
    }

    public boolean enQueue(int value) {
        if (size == data.length) {
            return false;
        }
        data[(head + size) % data.length] = value;  // next free slot, wrapping
        size += 1;
        return true;
    }

    public boolean deQueue() {
        if (size == 0) {
            return false;
        }
        head = (head + 1) % data.length;  // the front moves forward
        size -= 1;
        return true;
    }

    public int Front() {
        return size > 0 ? data[head] : -1;
    }

    public int Rear() {
        return size > 0 ? data[(head + size - 1) % data.length] : -1;
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    public boolean isFull() {
        return size == data.length;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Keeping size avoids the classic full-vs-empty ambiguity of head/tail pointers.
  2. All operations are O(1) index arithmetic.

  • Enqueue when full → false.
  • Dequeue when empty → false.
  • Wrap-around after many operations.

Complexity: O(1) per operation, O(k) space.

Medium 636. Exclusive Time of Functions Google Meta StringStack

Problem: Given start/end logs of a single-threaded program, return each function's exclusive running time.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 2, logs = ["0:start:0","1:start:2","1:end:5","0:end:6"]
Output: [3,4]
Explanation: Function 0 starts at the beginning of time 0, then it executes 2 for units of time and reaches the end of time 1. Function 1 starts at the beginning of time 2, executes for 4 units of time, and ends at the end of time 5. Function 0 resumes execution at the beginning of time 6 and executes for 1 unit of time. So function 0 spends 2 + 1 = 3 units of total time executing, and function 1 spends 4 units of total time executing.
Example 2
Input: n = 1, logs = ["0:start:0","0:start:2","0:end:5","0:start:6","0:end:6","0:end:7"]
Output: [8]
Explanation: Function 0 starts at the beginning of time 0, executes for 2 units of time, and recursively calls itself. Function 0 (recursive call) starts at the beginning of time 2 and executes for 4 units of time. Function 0 (initial call) resumes execution then immediately calls itself again. Function 0 (2nd recursive call) starts at the beginning of time 6 and executes for 1 unit of time. Function 0 (initial call) resumes execution at the beginning of time 7 and executes for 1 unit of time. So function 0 spends 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 8 units of total time executing.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 · 2 ≤ logs.length ≤ 500 · 0 ≤ function_id < n · 0 ≤ timestamp ≤ 10⁹ · No two start events will happen at the same timestamp. · No two end events will happen at the same timestamp. · Each function has an "end" log for each "start" log.

Hint 1

Which function is running between two consecutive log entries?

Hint 2

Keep a stack of active calls.

From brute force to the pattern: Computing each call's total duration and subtracting nested calls is more complicated; charging slices to the stack top is one pass.

Spot it: Function calls nest → a stack mirrors the call stack. Time between two events belongs to whichever function is on top.

Why not another pattern? Subtracting children's durations from parents afterwards needs extra bookkeeping per call.

Approach:

  1. Keep prev = the time the current slice started.
  2. start at t: charge t − prev to the top (if any), push the id, prev = t.
  3. end at t: charge t − prev + 1 to the top, pop, prev = t + 1.
class Solution:
    def exclusiveTime(self, n: int, logs: List[str]) -> List[int]:
        result = [0] * n
        stack = []
        prev = 0  # start of the current time slice
        for log in logs:
            fid, kind, t = log.split(":")
            fid, t = int(fid), int(t)
            if kind == "start":
                if stack:
                    result[stack[-1]] += t - prev  # the caller ran until now
                stack.append(fid)
                prev = t
            else:
                result[stack.pop()] += t - prev + 1  # end times are inclusive
                prev = t + 1
        return result
function exclusiveTime(n: number, logs: string[]): number[] {
    const result: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    const stack: number[] = [];
    let prev = 0;  // start of the current time slice
    for (const log of logs) {
        const [fidText, kind, tText] = log.split(":");
        const fid = Number(fidText), t = Number(tText);
        if (kind === "start") {
            if (stack.length > 0) {
                result[stack[stack.length - 1]] += t - prev;  // the caller ran until now
            }
            stack.push(fid);
            prev = t;
        } else {
            result[stack.pop()!] += t - prev + 1;  // end times are inclusive
            prev = t + 1;
        }
    }
    return result;
}
class Solution {
    public int[] exclusiveTime(int n, List<String> logs) {
        int[] result = new int[n];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int prev = 0;  // start of the current time slice
        for (String log : logs) {
            String[] parts = log.split(":");
            int fid = Integer.parseInt(parts[0]), t = Integer.parseInt(parts[2]);
            if (parts[1].equals("start")) {
                if (!stack.isEmpty()) {
                    result[stack.peek()] += t - prev;  // the caller ran until now
                }
                stack.push(fid);
                prev = t;
            } else {
                result[stack.pop()] += t - prev + 1;  // end times are inclusive
                prev = t + 1;
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A start pauses the current top; an end finishes it.
  2. End timestamps are inclusive (the function runs through the end of that unit), hence + 1.

  • A function that starts and ends at the same time unit.
  • Single function.

Complexity: O(len(logs)) time, O(n) space.

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ value ≤ 1000 · At most 2000 calls will be made to insertFront, insertLast, deleteFront, deleteLast, getFront, getRear, isEmpty, isFull.

Hint 1

Start from the circular queue design.

Hint 2

How does the head index move when inserting at the front?

From brute force to the pattern: List-based front inserts are O(n); the ring buffer is O(1).

Spot it: Same ring buffer as the circular queue, but the front can also move backwards: head = (head − 1) % k.

Why not another pattern? A list with insert(0, x) is O(n) per front insert.

Approach:

  1. insertFront: head = (head − 1) % k, write there.
  2. insertLast: write at (head + size) % k.
  3. deleteFront: head += 1; deleteLast: just size −= 1.
class MyCircularDeque:
    def __init__(self, k: int):
        self.data = [0] * k
        self.head = 0
        self.size = 0

    def insertFront(self, value: int) -> bool:
        if self.isFull():
            return False
        self.head = (self.head - 1) % len(self.data)  # step back, wrapping
        self.data[self.head] = value
        self.size += 1
        return True

    def insertLast(self, value: int) -> bool:
        if self.isFull():
            return False
        self.data[(self.head + self.size) % len(self.data)] = value
        self.size += 1
        return True

    def deleteFront(self) -> bool:
        if self.isEmpty():
            return False
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % len(self.data)
        self.size -= 1
        return True

    def deleteLast(self) -> bool:
        if self.isEmpty():
            return False
        self.size -= 1  # the last slot is simply forgotten
        return True

    def getFront(self) -> int:
        return -1 if self.isEmpty() else self.data[self.head]

    def getRear(self) -> int:
        return -1 if self.isEmpty() else self.data[(self.head + self.size - 1) % len(self.data)]

    def isEmpty(self) -> bool:
        return self.size == 0

    def isFull(self) -> bool:
        return self.size == len(self.data)

        this.data[this.head] = value;
        this.size += 1;

    insertLast(value: number): boolean {

class MyCircularDeque {
    private final int[] data;
    private int head = 0;
    private int size = 0;

    public MyCircularDeque(int k) {
        data = new int[k];
    }

    public boolean insertFront(int value) {
        if (isFull()) {
            return false;
        }
        head = (head - 1 + data.length) % data.length;  // step back, wrapping
        data[head] = value;
        size += 1;
        return true;
    }

    public boolean insertLast(int value) {
        if (isFull()) {
            return false;
        }
        data[(head + size) % data.length] = value;
        size += 1;
        return true;
    }

    public boolean deleteFront() {
        if (isEmpty()) {
            return false;
        }
        head = (head + 1) % data.length;
        size -= 1;
        return true;
    }

    public boolean deleteLast() {
        if (isEmpty()) {
            return false;
        }
        size -= 1;  // the last slot is simply forgotten
        return true;
    }

    public int getFront() {
        return isEmpty() ? -1 : data[head];
    }

    public int getRear() {
        return isEmpty() ? -1 : data[(head + size - 1) % data.length];
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    public boolean isFull() {
        return size == data.length;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Python's % returns a non-negative result, so (head − 1) % k wraps correctly.
  2. Removing from the back only shrinks the size.

Instead of one balance, track the minimum and maximum possible balance.

Hint 2

When is it impossible? When is it valid at the end?

From brute force to the pattern: Trying all star replacements is 3^k; the range is one pass. (Two stacks of indices also work in O(n).)

Spot it: A plain stack/counter would check balance; with wildcards, keep the range of possible open counts: lo (treat stars as )) and hi (treat stars as (). It's valid if hi never drops below 0 and lo can reach 0 at the end.

Why not another pattern? Trying three options for every star is 3^stars.

class Solution:
    def checkValidString(self, s: str) -> bool:
        lo = hi = 0  # range of possible numbers of unmatched "("
        for ch in s:
            if ch == "(":
                lo += 1
                hi += 1
            elif ch == ")":
                lo -= 1
                hi -= 1
            else:
                lo -= 1  # star as ")"
                hi += 1  # star as "("
            if hi < 0:
                return False  # too many ")" even with every star as "("
            lo = max(lo, 0)  # can't have negative open brackets
        return lo == 0
function checkValidString(s: string): boolean {
    let lo = 0, hi = 0;  // range of possible numbers of unmatched "("
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch === "(") {
            lo += 1;
            hi += 1;
        } else if (ch === ")") {
            lo -= 1;
            hi -= 1;
        } else {
            lo -= 1;  // star as ")"
            hi += 1;  // star as "("
        }
        if (hi < 0) {
            return false;  // too many ")" even with every star as "("
        }
        lo = Math.max(lo, 0);  // can't have negative open brackets
    }
    return lo === 0;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean checkValidString(String s) {
        int lo = 0, hi = 0;  // range of possible numbers of unmatched '('
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (ch == '(') {
                lo += 1;
                hi += 1;
            } else if (ch == ')') {
                lo -= 1;
                hi -= 1;
            } else {
                lo -= 1;  // star as ')'
                hi += 1;  // star as '('
            }
            if (hi < 0) {
                return false;  // too many ')' even with every star as '('
            }
            lo = Math.max(lo, 0);  // can't have negative open brackets
        }
        return lo == 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Every count between lo and hi is achievable by some choice of stars.
  2. Clamping lo at 0 discards choices that would make the prefix invalid.
  3. At the end, 0 open brackets must be achievable.

Medium 735. Asteroid Collision Google Meta Amazon Microsoft ArrayStack

Problem: Positive asteroids move right, negative move left; on collision the smaller explodes (equal: both). Return the survivors.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: asteroids = [5,10,-5]
Output: [5,10]
Explanation: The 10 and -5 collide resulting in 10. The 5 and 10 never collide.
Example 2
Input: asteroids = [8,-8]
Output: []
Explanation: The 8 and -8 collide exploding each other.

Constraints: 2 ≤ asteroids.length ≤ 10⁴ · -1000 ≤ asteroids[i] ≤ 1000 · asteroids[i] != 0

Hint 1

Which asteroids can collide? Only a left-mover with right-movers before it.

Hint 2

Use a stack of survivors.

From brute force to the pattern: Time-step simulation is slow; the stack resolves each collision once.

Spot it: Only a left-mover meeting earlier right-movers collides, and it meets the most recent first → a stack.

Why not another pattern? Simulating step by step in time is O(n²) or worse.

Approach:

  1. For each asteroid a: while a < 0 and the top is positive: compare sizes.
  2. Top smaller → pop, continue; equal → pop, a dies; top bigger → a dies.
  3. If a survives, push it.
class Solution:
    def asteroidCollision(self, asteroids: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        stack = []
        for a in asteroids:
            alive = True
            while alive and a < 0 and stack and stack[-1] > 0:  # a moving left meets one moving right
                if stack[-1] < -a:
                    stack.pop()  # the right-mover explodes; keep going
                    continue
                if stack[-1] == -a:
                    stack.pop()  # both explode
                alive = False  # a explodes
            if alive:
                stack.append(a)
        return stack
function asteroidCollision(asteroids: number[]): number[] {
    const stack: number[] = [];
    for (const a of asteroids) {
        let alive = true;
        while (alive && a < 0 && stack.length > 0 && stack[stack.length - 1] > 0) {  // a moving left meets one moving right
            if (stack[stack.length - 1] < -a) {
                stack.pop();  // the right-mover explodes; keep going
                continue;
            }
            if (stack[stack.length - 1] === -a) {
                stack.pop();  // both explode
            }
            alive = false;  // a explodes
        }
        if (alive) {
            stack.push(a);
        }
    }
    return stack;
}
class Solution {
    public int[] asteroidCollision(int[] asteroids) {
        List<Integer> stack = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int a : asteroids) {
            boolean alive = true;
            while (alive && a < 0 && !stack.isEmpty() && stack.get(stack.size() - 1) > 0) {  // a moving left meets one moving right
                int top = stack.get(stack.size() - 1);
                if (top < -a) {
                    stack.remove(stack.size() - 1);  // the right-mover explodes; keep going
                    continue;
                }
                if (top == -a) {
                    stack.remove(stack.size() - 1);  // both explode
                }
                alive = false;  // a explodes
            }
            if (alive) {
                stack.add(a);
            }
        }
        return stack.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Right-movers and left-movers that are already past each other never collide.
  2. A big left-mover may destroy several right-movers in a row.

  • Equal sizes (both explode).
  • All moving the same way.
  • Left-movers at the start (never collide).

Complexity: O(n) time (each asteroid pushed and popped at most once), O(n) space.

function minAddToMakeValid(s: string): number {

        } else if (openCount) {

        } else {

class Solution {

    def buildArray(self, target: List[int], n: int) -> List[str]:

Hard 224. Basic Calculator Google Meta Amazon Microsoft StringStack

Problem: Evaluate an expression with +, −, parentheses, spaces and unary minus (no eval).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "1 + 1"
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: s = " 2-1 + 2 "
Output: 3

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 3 * 10⁵ · s consists of digits, '+', '-', '(', ')', and ' '. · s represents a valid expression. · '+' is not used as a unary operation (i.e., "+1" and "+(2 + 3)" is invalid). · '-' could be used as a unary operation (i.e., "-1" and "-(2 + 3)" is valid). · There will be no two consecutive operators in the input. · Every number and running calculation will fit in a signed 32-bit integer.

Hint 1

With only + and −, what do you need to remember besides the running total?

Hint 2

When you see '(', save the current total and sign; restore them at ')'.

From brute force to the pattern: Repeatedly evaluating the innermost brackets with string rewriting is O(n²); the stack is one pass.

Spot it: Without ×/÷, only signs matter. Keep a running result and the current sign. A parenthesis starts a fresh sub-result; save the outer state on a stack and combine when it closes.

Why not another pattern? Converting to postfix (shunting-yard) works but is longer; recursion works but the stack makes the state explicit.

Approach:

  1. Digits build num.
  2. On +/−: result += sign · num, reset num, set sign.
  3. On (: push result and sign, reset both.
  4. On ): finish the inner result, then result = pushed_result + pushed_sign · result.
class Solution:
    def calculate(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = []
        result = 0
        num = 0
        sign = 1
        for ch in s:
            if ch.isdigit():
                num = num * 10 + int(ch)
            elif ch in "+-":
                result += sign * num  # finish the previous number
                num = 0
                sign = 1 if ch == "+" else -1
            elif ch == "(":
                stack.append(result)  # save the outer state
                stack.append(sign)
                result = 0
                sign = 1
            elif ch == ")":
                result += sign * num
                num = 0
                outer_sign = stack.pop()
                result = stack.pop() + outer_sign * result  # plug the bracket into the outer expression
        return result + sign * num
function calculate(s: string): number {
    const stack: number[] = [];
    let result = 0;
    let num = 0;
    let sign = 1;
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch >= "0" && ch <= "9") {
            num = num * 10 + Number(ch);
        } else if (ch === "+" || ch === "-") {
            result += sign * num;  // finish the previous number
            num = 0;
            sign = ch === "+" ? 1 : -1;
        } else if (ch === "(") {
            stack.push(result);  // save the outer state
            stack.push(sign);
            result = 0;
            sign = 1;
        } else if (ch === ")") {
            result += sign * num;
            num = 0;
            const outerSign = stack.pop()!;
            result = stack.pop()! + outerSign * result;  // plug the bracket into the outer expression
        }
    }
    return result + sign * num;
}
class Solution {
    public int calculate(String s) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int result = 0;
        int num = 0;
        int sign = 1;
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isDigit(ch)) {
                num = num * 10 + (ch - '0');
            } else if (ch == '+' || ch == '-') {
                result += sign * num;  // finish the previous number
                num = 0;
                sign = ch == '+' ? 1 : -1;
            } else if (ch == '(') {
                stack.push(result);  // save the outer state
                stack.push(sign);
                result = 0;
                sign = 1;
            } else if (ch == ')') {
                result += sign * num;
                num = 0;
                int outerSign = stack.pop();
                result = stack.pop() + outerSign * result;  // plug the bracket into the outer expression
            }
        }
        return result + sign * num;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A unary minus like -(2+3) just sets sign = −1 before the bracket, which multiplies the whole bracket's value.
  2. Each bracket level has its own running result; the stack remembers the levels outside it.

  • Nested brackets.
  • Spaces everywhere.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(depth) space.

Medium 856. Score of Parentheses Meta StringStack

Problem: Score a balanced string: () is 1, AB is A + B, (A) is 2 · A.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "()"
Output: 1
Example 2
Input: s = "(())"
Output: 2

Constraints: 2 ≤ s.length ≤ 50 · s consists of only '(' and ')'. · s is a balanced parentheses string.

Hint 1

Keep a score for every open level of nesting.

Hint 2

When a group closes, how do you turn its inside score into its own score?

From brute force to the pattern: Recursive splitting of substrings is O(n²); the stack is one pass. (A depth-counting trick even gets O(1) space.)

Spot it: Nested structure evaluated from the inside out → a stack holding the running score of each open level.

Why not another pattern? Recursing on substrings re-scans them; the stack does it in one pass.

Approach:

  1. Start with [0] (the outer level).
  2. (: push 0 (a new level).
  3. ): pop v; add max(2 · v, 1) to the new top (() is 1, (A) is 2A).
class Solution:
    def scoreOfParentheses(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = [0]  # score accumulated at each open depth
        for ch in s:
            if ch == "(":
                stack.append(0)  # start a new group
            else:
                inner = stack.pop()
                stack[-1] += max(2 * inner, 1)  # "()" scores 1, "(A)" doubles A
        return stack[0]
function scoreOfParentheses(s: string): number {
    const stack: number[] = [0];  // score accumulated at each open depth
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch === "(") {
            stack.push(0);  // start a new group
        } else {
            const inner = stack.pop()!;
            stack[stack.length - 1] += Math.max(2 * inner, 1);  // "()" scores 1, "(A)" doubles A
        }
    }
    return stack[0];
}
class Solution {
    public int scoreOfParentheses(String s) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();  // score accumulated at each open depth
        stack.push(0);
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (ch == '(') {
                stack.push(0);  // start a new group
            } else {
                int inner = stack.pop();
                stack.push(stack.pop() + Math.max(2 * inner, 1));  // "()" scores 1, "(A)" doubles A
            }
        }
        return stack.peek();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each stack entry is the score of the group currently open at that depth.
  2. Closing a group turns its inner score into the group's score and adds it to its parent (the A + B rule).

  • Deep nesting ((())) → 4.
  • Side by side ()() → 2.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(depth) space.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Output: "lee(t(c)o)de"

Example 2
Input: s = "a)b(c)d"
Output: "ab(c)d"

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s[i] is either '(' , ')', or lowercase English letter.

Hint 1

Which ) can never be matched?

Hint 2

Track the indices of unmatched ( with a stack; whatever remains at the end must go.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying subsets of brackets to remove is exponential; one stack pass removes exactly the unmatched ones.

Spot it: Matching brackets → a stack. A ) with nothing open can never be matched, so drop it right away. Any ( still on the stack at the end never got closed, so drop those too. Everything else is kept, which is the minimum removal.

Why not another pattern? Trying removal subsets (as in Remove Invalid Parentheses) is exponential; here any one valid answer is enough, so a single pass works.

Approach:

  1. Scan left to right with a stack of indices of unmatched (.
  2. ) with an empty stack → mark its index for removal; otherwise pop.
  3. After the scan, the indices left on the stack are unmatched (: remove them too.
class Solution:
    def minRemoveToMakeValid(self, s: str) -> str:
        chars = list(s)
        stack = []  # indices of "(" waiting for a match
        for i, ch in enumerate(chars):
            if ch == "(":
                stack.append(i)
            elif ch == ")":
                if stack:
                    stack.pop()  # matched
                else:
                    chars[i] = ""  # nothing to close: remove it
        for i in stack:
            chars[i] = ""  # "(" that never closed
        return "".join(chars)
function minRemoveToMakeValid(s: string): string {
    const chars = [...s];
    const stack: number[] = [];  // indices of "(" waiting for a match
    chars.forEach((ch, i) => {
        if (ch === "(") {
            stack.push(i);
        } else if (ch === ")") {
            if (stack.length > 0) {
                stack.pop();  // matched
            } else {
                chars[i] = "";  // nothing to close: remove it
            }
        }
    });
    for (const i of stack) {
        chars[i] = "";  // "(" that never closed
    }
    return chars.join("");
}
class Solution {
    public String minRemoveToMakeValid(String s) {
        char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();  // indices of '(' waiting for a match
        for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) {
            if (chars[i] == '(') {
                stack.push(i);
            } else if (chars[i] == ')') {
                if (!stack.isEmpty()) {
                    stack.pop();  // matched
                } else {
                    chars[i] = 0;  // nothing to close: remove it (0 marks "removed")
                }
            }
        }
        for (int i : stack) {
            chars[i] = 0;  // '(' that never closed
        }
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (char ch : chars) {
            if (ch != 0) {
                out.append(ch);
            }
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Every removed ) had no ( before it to pair with, so removing it is unavoidable.
  2. Every removed ( had no ) after it, so it's unavoidable too; nothing else is removed.
  3. Blanking characters in a list and joining once keeps it O(n).
