Medium 1209. Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String II Amazon StringStack

Problem: Repeatedly remove k adjacent equal letters until no more removals are possible.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abcd", k = 2
Output: "abcd"
Explanation: There's nothing to delete.
Example 2
Input: s = "deeedbbcccbdaa", k = 3
Output: "aa"
Explanation: First delete "eee" and "ccc", get "ddbbbdaa" Then delete "bbb", get "dddaa" Finally delete "ddd", get "aa"

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · 2 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴ · s only contains lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

What happens around a removed group?

Hint 2

Keep runs of equal characters on a stack.

From brute force to the pattern: Repeated scanning is quadratic; the run stack is linear.

Spot it: Removals can cascade (removing a run joins its neighbours), which a stack handles naturally: keep runs as (char, count).

Why not another pattern? Rescanning the string after each removal is O(n² / k).

Approach:

  1. For each ch: if it matches the top run, increment; else push (ch, 1).
  2. When the top count reaches k, pop it.
  3. Rebuild the string from the stack.
class Solution:
    def removeDuplicates(self, s: str, k: int) -> str:
        stack = []  # [char, run length]
        for ch in s:
            if stack and stack[-1][0] == ch:
                stack[-1][1] += 1
                if stack[-1][1] == k:
                    stack.pop()  # k in a row disappear
            else:
                stack.append([ch, 1])
        return "".join(ch * count for ch, count in stack)
function removeDuplicates(s: string, k: number): string {
    const stack: [string, number][] = [];  // [char, run length]
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (stack.length > 0 && stack[stack.length - 1][0] === ch) {
            stack[stack.length - 1][1] += 1;
            if (stack[stack.length - 1][1] === k) {
                stack.pop();  // k in a row disappear
            }
        } else {
            stack.push([ch, 1]);
        }
    }
    return stack.map(([ch, count]) => ch.repeat(count)).join("");
}
class Solution {
    public String removeDuplicates(String s, int k) {
        List<int[]> stack = new ArrayList<>();  // (char, run length)
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.get(stack.size() - 1)[0] == ch) {
                stack.get(stack.size() - 1)[1] += 1;
                if (stack.get(stack.size() - 1)[1] == k) {
                    stack.remove(stack.size() - 1);  // k in a row disappear
                }
            } else {
                stack.add(new int[] {ch, 1});
            }
        }
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (int[] run : stack) {
            out.append(String.valueOf((char) run[0]).repeat(run[1]));
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. After popping a run, the next character compares with the run below, so cascades happen automatically.
  2. Each character is pushed and popped at most once.

Output: "dab"
Explanation: The following operations are done: - s = "daabcbaabcbc", remove "abc" starting at index 2, so s = "dabaabcbc". - s = "dabaabcbc", remove "abc" starting at index 4, so s = "dababc". - s = "dababc", remove "abc" starting at index 3, so s = "dab". Now s has no occurrences of "abc".
Example 2
Input: s = "axxxxyyyyb", part = "xy"
Output: "ab"
Explanation: The following operations are done: - s = "axxxxyyyyb", remove "xy" starting at index 4 so s = "axxxyyyb". - s = "axxxyyyb", remove "xy" starting at index 3 so s = "axxyyb". - s = "axxyyb", remove "xy" starting at index 2 so s = "axyb". - s = "axyb", remove "xy" starting at index 1 so s = "ab". Now s has no occurrences of "xy".

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000 · 1 ≤ part.length ≤ 1000 · s and part consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Process the string left to right.

Hint 2

Use a stack and check its top after each push.

From brute force to the pattern: Repeated find-and-remove restarts each time; the stack does one pass.

Spot it: Removing the leftmost occurrence and continuing is the same as scanning left to right with a stack and deleting part as soon as it appears at the top.

Why not another pattern? Calling replace/find in a loop restarts the scan every time.

Approach:

  1. Append each character to out.
  2. If out ends with part, delete those characters.
class Solution:
    def removeOccurrences(self, s: str, part: str) -> str:
        out = []
        L = len(part)
        for ch in s:
            out.append(ch)
            if len(out) >= L and "".join(out[-L:]) == part:
                del out[-L:]  # remove the occurrence just completed
        return "".join(out)
function removeOccurrences(s: string, part: string): string {
    const out: string[] = [];
    const L = part.length;
    for (const ch of s) {
        out.push(ch);
        if (out.length >= L && out.slice(-L).join("") === part) {
            out.splice(out.length - L, L);  // remove the occurrence just completed
        }
    }
    return out.join("");
}
class Solution {
    public String removeOccurrences(String s, String part) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        int L = part.length();
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            out.append(ch);
            if (out.length() >= L && out.substring(out.length() - L).equals(part)) {
                out.setLength(out.length() - L);  // remove the occurrence just completed
            }
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The first occurrence to complete while scanning is the leftmost one in the current string.
  2. Deleting from the top lets earlier characters join with later ones, like the real process.

The input is tiny: just simulate.

From brute force to the pattern: This is the simulation.

Spot it: With |s| ≤ 20 the string stays small: a direct simulation, using a list as a stack (append and pop at the end).

Why not another pattern? Version II needs reverse reasoning because the result can reach 10¹⁵ characters; here it can't.

Approach:

  1. Letter → append; * → pop if non-empty; # → res += res; % → res.reverse().
class Solution:
    def processStr(self, s: str) -> str:
        res = []
        for ch in s:
            if ch == "*":
                if res:
                    res.pop()  # delete the last character
            elif ch == "#":
                res += res  # duplicate
            elif ch == "%":
                res.reverse()
            else:
                res.append(ch)
        return "".join(res)
function processStr(s: string): string {
    let res: string[] = [];
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch === "*") {
            if (res.length > 0) {
                res.pop();  // delete the last character
            }
        } else if (ch === "#") {
            res = res.concat(res);  // duplicate
        } else if (ch === "%") {
            res.reverse();
        } else {
            res.push(ch);
        }
    }
    return res.join("");
}
class Solution {
    public String processStr(String s) {
        StringBuilder res = new StringBuilder();
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (ch == '*') {
                if (res.length() > 0) {
                    res.deleteCharAt(res.length() - 1);  // delete the last character
                }
            } else if (ch == '#') {
                res.append(res.toString());  // duplicate
            } else if (ch == '%') {
                res.reverse();
            } else {
                res.append(ch);
            }
        }
        return res.toString();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A list makes append and pop O(1).
  2. Duplication can double the length at most 20 times: up to 2²⁰ characters, still fine.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • * on an empty result.
  • Several # in a row.
  • Reverse then delete.

Complexity: O(final length · |s|) time in the worst case.

Hard 726. Number of Atoms Amazon StringStackHash Map

Problem: Count the atoms in a chemical formula with nested parentheses and multipliers; return them sorted with counts.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: formula = "H2O"
Output: "H2O"
Explanation: The count of elements are {'H': 2, 'O': 1}.
Example 2
Input: formula = "Mg(OH)2"
Output: "H2MgO2"
Explanation: The count of elements are {'H': 2, 'Mg': 1, 'O': 2}.

Constraints: 1 ≤ formula.length ≤ 1000 · formula consists of English letters, digits, '(', and ')'. · formula is always valid.

Hint 1

Parentheses nest: what structure handles that?

Hint 2

Keep a counter per open group; multiply when it closes.

From brute force to the pattern: Expanding the formula is exponential in nesting; stacked counters are near-linear.

Spot it: Nested groups → a stack of counters (hash maps). Closing a group multiplies its counts and adds them to the enclosing group.

Why not another pattern? Recursion works too; string expansion of multipliers explodes.

Approach:

  1. Atom: an uppercase letter plus lowercase letters, then an optional number.
  2. (: push a new counter. ) + number: pop, multiply, merge into the top.
  3. Format sorted names with counts > 1.
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def countOfAtoms(self, formula: str) -> str:
        stack = [Counter()]
        i, n = 0, len(formula)

        def read_number():
            nonlocal i
            start = i
            while i < n and formula[i].isdigit():
                i += 1
            return int(formula[start:i]) if i > start else 1

        while i < n:
            ch = formula[i]
            if ch == "(":
                stack.append(Counter())  # a new group starts
                i += 1
            elif ch == ")":
                i += 1
                mult = read_number()
                group = stack.pop()
                for atom, c in group.items():
                    stack[-1][atom] += c * mult  # multiply and fold into the enclosing group
            else:
                start = i
                i += 1
                while i < n and formula[i].islower():
                    i += 1
                atom = formula[start:i]
                stack[-1][atom] += read_number()
        counts = stack[0]
        return "".join(a + (str(counts[a]) if counts[a] > 1 else "") for a in sorted(counts))
function countOfAtoms(formula: string): string {
    const stack: Map<string, number>[] = [new Map()];
    let i = 0;
    const n = formula.length;
    const isDigit = (ch: string): boolean => ch >= "0" && ch <= "9";

    const readNumber = (): number => {
        const start = i;
        while (i < n && isDigit(formula[i])) {
            i += 1;
        }
        return i > start ? Number(formula.slice(start, i)) : 1;
    };

    const add = (group: Map<string, number>, atom: string, c: number): void => {
        group.set(atom, (group.get(atom) ?? 0) + c);
    };

    while (i < n) {
        const ch = formula[i];
        if (ch === "(") {
            stack.push(new Map());  // a new group starts
            i += 1;
        } else if (ch === ")") {
            i += 1;
            const mult = readNumber();
            const group = stack.pop()!;
            for (const [atom, c] of group) {
                add(stack[stack.length - 1], atom, c * mult);  // multiply and fold into the enclosing group
            }
        } else {
            const start = i;
            i += 1;
            while (i < n && formula[i] >= "a" && formula[i] <= "z") {
                i += 1;
            }
            const atom = formula.slice(start, i);
            add(stack[stack.length - 1], atom, readNumber());
        }
    }
    const counts = stack[0];
    return [...counts.keys()].sort().map((a) => a + (counts.get(a)! > 1 ? String(counts.get(a)) : "")).join("");
}
class Solution {
    private String formula;
    private int i;

    public String countOfAtoms(String formula) {
        this.formula = formula;
        i = 0;
        int n = formula.length();
        Deque<Map<String, Integer>> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        stack.push(new HashMap<>());
        while (i < n) {
            char ch = formula.charAt(i);
            if (ch == '(') {
                stack.push(new HashMap<>());  // a new group starts
                i += 1;
            } else if (ch == ')') {
                i += 1;
                int mult = readNumber();
                Map<String, Integer> group = stack.pop();
                for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : group.entrySet()) {
                    stack.peek().merge(e.getKey(), e.getValue() * mult, Integer::sum);  // multiply and fold into the enclosing group
                }
            } else {
                int start = i;
                i += 1;
                while (i < n && Character.isLowerCase(formula.charAt(i))) {
                    i += 1;
                }
                String atom = formula.substring(start, i);
                stack.peek().merge(atom, readNumber(), Integer::sum);
            }
        }
        TreeMap<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>(stack.peek());  // atoms in sorted order
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : counts.entrySet()) {
            out.append(e.getKey());
            if (e.getValue() > 1) {
                out.append(e.getValue());
            }
        }
        return out.toString();
    }

    private int readNumber() {
        int start = i;
        while (i < formula.length() && Character.isDigit(formula.charAt(i))) {
            i += 1;
        }
        return i > start ? Integer.parseInt(formula.substring(start, i)) : 1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each counter holds the atoms of one open group.
  2. A missing number means 1.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Nested parentheses.
  • Multi-letter atoms (Mg).
  • No numbers.

Complexity: O(n · depth) time in the worst case, O(n) space.

Hard 2751. Robot Collisions Amazon ArrayStack

Problem: Robots move left or right with health values; on collision the weaker is removed and the stronger loses 1 (equal: both removed). Return survivors' health in input order.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: positions = [5,4,3,2,1], healths = [2,17,9,15,10], directions = "RRRRR"
Output: [2,17,9,15,10]
Explanation: No collision occurs in this example, since all robots are moving in the same direction. So, the health of the robots in order from the first robot is returned, [2, 17, 9, 15, 10].
Example 2
Input: positions = [3,5,2,6], healths = [10,10,15,12], directions = "RLRL"
Output: [14]
Explanation: There are 2 collisions in this example. Firstly, robot 1 and robot 2 will collide, and since both have the same health, they will be removed from the line. Next, robot 3 and robot 4 will collide and since robot 4's health is smaller, it gets removed, and robot 3's health becomes 15 - 1 = 14. Only robot 3 remains, so we return [14].

Constraints: 1 ≤ positions.length == healths.length == directions.length == n ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ positions[i], healths[i] ≤ 10⁹ · directions[i] == 'L' or directions[i] == 'R' · All values in positions are distinct

Hint 1

Sort by position. Who can collide?

Hint 2

Use a stack of right-movers, as in Asteroid Collision.

From brute force to the pattern: Time-step simulation is slow; the stack resolves each collision once.

Spot it: Like Asteroid Collision: sort by position, and a left-mover meets the most recent right-movers first → a stack.

Why not another pattern? Simulating time steps is slow and positions can be far apart.

Approach:

  1. Process robots by position; right-movers go on the stack.
  2. A left-mover fights the stack top: the weaker dies, the stronger loses 1; equal → both die.
  3. Collect survivors and output by original index.
class Solution:
    def survivedRobotsHealths(self, positions: List[int], healths: List[int], directions: str) -> List[int]:
        health = healths[:]
        stack = []  # indices of robots moving right
        for i in sorted(range(len(positions)), key=lambda i: positions[i]):
            if directions[i] == "R":
                stack.append(i)
                continue
            while stack and health[i] > 0:
                j = stack[-1]
                if health[j] < health[i]:
                    health[j] = 0  # right-mover dies
                    stack.pop()
                    health[i] -= 1
                elif health[j] > health[i]:
                    health[i] = 0  # left-mover dies
                    health[j] -= 1
                else:
                    health[i] = health[j] = 0  # both die
                    stack.pop()
        return [h for h in health if h > 0]  # original order
function survivedRobotsHealths(positions: number[], healths: number[], directions: string): number[] {
    const health = [...healths];
    const stack: number[] = [];  // indices of robots moving right
    const order = positions.map((_, i) => i).sort((a, b) => positions[a] - positions[b]);
    for (const i of order) {
        if (directions[i] === "R") {
            stack.push(i);
            continue;
        }
        while (stack.length > 0 && health[i] > 0) {
            const j = stack[stack.length - 1];
            if (health[j] < health[i]) {
                health[j] = 0;  // right-mover dies
                stack.pop();
                health[i] -= 1;
            } else if (health[j] > health[i]) {
                health[i] = 0;  // left-mover dies
                health[j] -= 1;
            } else {
                health[i] = 0;  // both die
                health[j] = 0;
                stack.pop();
            }
        }
    }
    return health.filter((h) => h > 0);  // original order
}
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> survivedRobotsHealths(int[] positions, int[] healths, String directions) {
        int[] health = healths.clone();
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();  // indices of robots moving right
        Integer[] order = new Integer[positions.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < order.length; i++) {
            order[i] = i;
        }
        Arrays.sort(order, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(positions[a], positions[b]));
        for (int i : order) {
            if (directions.charAt(i) == 'R') {
                stack.push(i);
                continue;
            }
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && health[i] > 0) {
                int j = stack.peek();
                if (health[j] < health[i]) {
                    health[j] = 0;  // right-mover dies
                    stack.pop();
                    health[i] -= 1;
                } else if (health[j] > health[i]) {
                    health[i] = 0;  // left-mover dies
                    health[j] -= 1;
                } else {
                    health[i] = 0;  // both die
                    health[j] = 0;
                    stack.pop();
                }
            }
        }
        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int h : health) {
            if (h > 0) {
                result.add(h);  // original order
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Robots facing the same way, or already past each other, never collide.
  2. A strong left-mover can defeat several right-movers in a row, losing 1 health each time.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Equal health (both removed).
  • All moving one way.
  • A left-mover surviving several fights.

Complexity: O(n log n) time (sorting), O(n) space.

Hard 3614. Process String with Special Operations II Amazon String

Problem: Same operations as version I, but the result can be 10¹⁵ long. Return the character at index k (or '.').

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "a#b%*", k = 1
Output: "a"
Explanation: i s[i] Operation Current result 0 'a' Append 'a' "a" 1 '#' Duplicate result "aa" 2 'b' Append 'b' "aab" 3 '%' Reverse result "baa" 4 '*' Remove the last character "ba" The final result is "ba". The character at index k = 1 is 'a'.
Example 2
Input: s = "cd%#*#", k = 3
Output: "d"
Explanation: i s[i] Operation Current result 0 'c' Append 'c' "c" 1 'd' Append 'd' "cd" 2 '%' Reverse result "dc" 3 '#' Duplicate result "dcdc" 4 '*' Remove the last character "dcd" 5 '#' Duplicate result "dcddcd" The final result is "dcddcd". The character at index k = 3 is 'd'.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s consists of only lowercase English letters and special characters '*', '#', and '%'. · 0 ≤ k ≤ 10¹⁵ · The length of result after processing s will not exceed 10¹⁵.

Hint 1

You can't build the string. Can you track only its length?

Hint 2

Walk the operations backwards and map k to its position before each operation.

From brute force to the pattern: Simulation needs up to 10¹⁵ characters; backward index mapping is O(|s|).

Spot it: Building the string is impossible. Record the length after each operation, then go backwards: each operation tells where index k came from (a duplicate maps k to k mod half, a reverse to len − 1 − k), until a letter operation produced it.

Why not another pattern? Simulation can need 10¹⁵ characters.

Approach:

  1. lens[i] = length after operation i.
  2. If k ≥ lens[-1], return '.'.
  3. Backwards: letter → if k is the last index, return it; # → k %= previous length; % → k = previous length − 1 − k; * → unchanged.
class Solution:
    def processStr(self, s: str, k: int) -> str:
        lens = []
        length = 0
        for ch in s:
            if ch == "*":
                length = max(0, length - 1)
            elif ch == "#":
                length *= 2
            elif ch != "%":
                length += 1  # a letter
            lens.append(length)
        if k >= length:
            return "."
        for i in range(len(s) - 1, -1, -1):
            ch = s[i]
            before = lens[i - 1] if i else 0
            if ch == "#":
                k %= before  # the second half copies the first
            elif ch == "%":
                k = before - 1 - k  # undo the reverse
            elif ch != "*" and k == lens[i] - 1:
                return ch  # this letter is exactly position k
        return "."
function processStr(s: string, k: number): string {
    const lens: number[] = [];
    let length = 0;
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch === "*") {
            length = Math.max(0, length - 1);
        } else if (ch === "#") {
            length *= 2;
        } else if (ch !== "%") {
            length += 1;  // a letter
        }
        lens.push(length);
    }
    if (k >= length) {
        return ".";
    }
    for (let i = s.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        const ch = s[i];
        const before = i ? lens[i - 1] : 0;
        if (ch === "#") {
            k %= before;  // the second half copies the first
        } else if (ch === "%") {
            k = before - 1 - k;  // undo the reverse
        } else if (ch !== "*" && k === lens[i] - 1) {
            return ch;  // this letter is exactly position k
        }
    }
    return ".";
}
class Solution {
    public char processStr(String s, long k) {
        long[] lens = new long[s.length()];
        long length = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char ch = s.charAt(i);
            if (ch == '*') {
                length = Math.max(0, length - 1);
            } else if (ch == '#') {
                length *= 2;
            } else if (ch != '%') {
                length += 1;  // a letter
            }
            lens[i] = length;
        }
        if (k >= length) {
            return '.';
        }
        for (int i = s.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            char ch = s.charAt(i);
            long before = i > 0 ? lens[i - 1] : 0;
            if (ch == '#') {
                k %= before;  // the second half copies the first
            } else if (ch == '%') {
                k = before - 1 - k;  // undo the reverse
            } else if (ch != '*' && k == lens[i] - 1) {
                return ch;  // this letter is exactly position k
            }
        }
        return '.';
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Deleting the last character never moves the others, so * doesn't change k (which is inside the shorter string).
  2. After #, index k in the doubled string is index k mod before in the original.
  3. A letter appended at position lens[i] − 1 is the answer if k points there; otherwise it came from earlier.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k out of range → '.'.
  • Many duplications.
  • Reverse right after duplication.

Complexity: O(|s|) time and space.

Hard 736. Parse Lisp Expression Apple StringStackHash Map

Problem: Evaluate a Lisp-like expression with let, add, mult, integers and lexically scoped variables.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: expression = "(let x 2 (mult x (let x 3 y 4 (add x y))))"
Output: 14
Explanation: In the expression (add x y), when checking for the value of the variable x, we check from the innermost scope to the outermost in the context of the variable we are trying to evaluate. Since x = 3 is found first, the value of x is 3.
Example 2
Input: expression = "(let x 3 x 2 x)"
Output: 2
Explanation: Assignment in let statements is processed sequentially.

Constraints: 1 ≤ expression.length ≤ 2000 · There are no leading or trailing spaces in expression. · All tokens are separated by a single space in expression. · The answer and all intermediate calculations of that answer are guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer. · The expression is guaranteed to be legal and evaluate to an integer.

Hint 1

Tokenise, then evaluate recursively.

Hint 2

Keep a stack of scopes for let; look variables up from the innermost scope outward.

From brute force to the pattern: String rewriting can't handle scopes; a recursive evaluator is the natural fit.

Spot it: Nested parentheses → evaluate recursively over tokens. Variable scoping is a stack of scopes (hash maps): let pushes a scope, assignments go into it, and lookups search from the innermost scope outwards.

Why not another pattern? Regex or string replacement can't handle shadowed variables and nesting correctly.

Approach:

  1. Tokenise: (, ) and words.
  2. evaluate(): a number or variable returns its value; ( reads the operator.
  3. add/mult: evaluate two sub-expressions. let: push a scope; while the next token is a variable followed by an expression, assign; the last expression is the value; pop the scope.
class Solution:
    def evaluate(self, expression: str) -> int:
        tokens = expression.replace("(", " ( ").replace(")", " ) ").split()
        self.i = 0
        scopes = [{}]  # innermost scope last

        def lookup(name):
            for scope in reversed(scopes):
                if name in scope:
                    return scope[name]  # the nearest enclosing assignment

        def value():
            tok = tokens[self.i]
            self.i += 1
            if tok != "(":
                return lookup(tok) if tok[0].isalpha() else int(tok)
            op = tokens[self.i]
            self.i += 1
            if op in ("add", "mult"):
                a = value()
                b = value()
                result = a + b if op == "add" else a * b
            else:  # let
                scopes.append({})
                while True:
                    tok = tokens[self.i]
                    if tok == "(" or not tok[0].isalpha() or tokens[self.i + 1] == ")":
                        result = value()  # the final expression
                        break
                    self.i += 1
                    scopes[-1][tok] = value()  # assign in this scope
                scopes.pop()
            self.i += 1  # skip ")"
            return result

        return value()
function evaluate(expression: string): number {
    const tokens = expression.replaceAll("(", " ( ").replaceAll(")", " ) ").split(" ").filter((t) => t.length > 0);
    let i = 0;
    const scopes: Map<string, number>[] = [new Map()];  // innermost scope last
    const isAlpha = (ch: string): boolean => /[a-z]/i.test(ch);

    const lookup = (name: string): number => {
        for (let s = scopes.length - 1; s >= 0; s--) {
            if (scopes[s].has(name)) {
                return scopes[s].get(name)!;  // the nearest enclosing assignment
            }
        }
        return 0;
    };

    const value = (): number => {
        const tok = tokens[i];
        i += 1;
        if (tok !== "(") {
            return isAlpha(tok[0]) ? lookup(tok) : Number(tok);
        }
        const op = tokens[i];
        i += 1;
        let result: number;
        if (op === "add" || op === "mult") {
            const a = value();
            const b = value();
            result = op === "add" ? a + b : a * b;
        } else {  // let
            scopes.push(new Map());
            while (true) {
                const t = tokens[i];
                if (t === "(" || !isAlpha(t[0]) || tokens[i + 1] === ")") {
                    result = value();  // the final expression
                    break;
                }
                i += 1;
                scopes[scopes.length - 1].set(t, value());  // assign in this scope
            }
            scopes.pop();
        }
        i += 1;  // skip ")"
        return result;
    };

    return value();
}
class Solution {
    private List<String> tokens;
    private int i;
    private Deque<Map<String, Integer>> scopes;  // innermost scope first

    public int evaluate(String expression) {
        tokens = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String t : expression.replace("(", " ( ").replace(")", " ) ").trim().split("\\s+")) {
            tokens.add(t);
        }
        i = 0;
        scopes = new ArrayDeque<>();
        scopes.push(new HashMap<>());
        return value();
    }

    private int lookup(String name) {
        for (Map<String, Integer> scope : scopes) {  // innermost first
            if (scope.containsKey(name)) {
                return scope.get(name);  // the nearest enclosing assignment
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }

    private int value() {
        String tok = tokens.get(i);
        i += 1;
        if (!tok.equals("(")) {
            return Character.isLetter(tok.charAt(0)) ? lookup(tok) : Integer.parseInt(tok);
        }
        String op = tokens.get(i);
        i += 1;
        int result;
        if (op.equals("add") || op.equals("mult")) {
            int a = value();
            int b = value();
            result = op.equals("add") ? a + b : a * b;
        } else {  // let
            scopes.push(new HashMap<>());
            while (true) {
                String t = tokens.get(i);
                if (t.equals("(") || !Character.isLetter(t.charAt(0)) || tokens.get(i + 1).equals(")")) {
                    result = value();  // the final expression
                    break;
                }
                i += 1;
                scopes.peek().put(t, value());  // assign in this scope
            }
            scopes.pop();
        }
        i += 1;  // skip ")"
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A let body is "variable value" pairs until a token that's an expression on its own: a (, a number, or a variable right before ).
  2. Assignments go into the innermost scope, so shadowing works and disappears when the let ends.
  3. Each token is consumed once, so evaluation is linear.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Shadowed variables.
  • Reassigning in the same let (let x 3 x 2 x).
  • Negative numbers.

Complexity: O(n · depth) time (scope lookups), O(n) space.
